data.hypothesis: Don't try to finish all math before coding. Learn linear algebra and basic stats now. Calculus intuition is enough — you don't need to hand-derive gradients.
data.methodology: Parallel track: study math concepts alongside coding exercises. Use visual resources (3Blue1Brown) for intuition, then immediately apply in NumPy/Pandas notebooks.
findings: Linear algebra — vectors, matrices, dot products, eigenvectors (intuition, not proofs)
Statistics & probability — distributions, Bayes, hypothesis testing
Calculus — derivatives, chain rule, gradient intuition only
Python for data — NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, Jupyter
Python advanced — decorators, generators, OOP, typing
data.conclusion: 🎯 Milestone: Build a Jupyter notebook that loads a CSV dataset, cleans it, runs descriptive stats, and plots 3 meaningful visualizations.

data.hypothesis: Don't skip classical ML to jump straight to deep learning. Interviewers ask about it. Many real-world problems are best solved with XGBoost, not a transformer.
data.methodology: Work through Andrew Ng's ML Specialization for theory, then immediately apply on Kaggle competitions for hands-on practice. Track experiments with MLflow.
findings: Supervised learning — regression, classification, decision trees, random forests, XGBoost
Unsupervised — clustering, PCA, dimensionality reduction
Model evaluation — train/val/test splits, cross-validation, ROC, precision/recall
scikit-learn end to end — pipelines, preprocessing, hyperparameter tuning
MLflow basics — experiment tracking
data.conclusion: 🎯 Milestone: Complete 2 Kaggle competitions. Place in top 50% on at least one. Push code to GitHub.

data.hypothesis: Karpathy's 'Neural Networks: Zero to Hero' series is genuinely the best resource on the internet for understanding LLMs from first principles. Watch it. Code along. Don't just watch — type every line.
data.methodology: Follow Karpathy's series as the spine. Use Jay Alammar's visual guides to build intuition. Implement everything in PyTorch. Read the Attention paper alongside the Illustrated Transformer.
findings: Neural networks from scratch — forward pass, backprop, gradient descent
CNNs, RNNs — understand the progression to transformers
Transformers & attention — the 'Attention is All You Need' paper (read alongside Karpathy)
PyTorch fundamentals — tensors, autograd, training loops
Hugging Face ecosystem — models, tokenizers, datasets, pipelines

references.text: ★ Karpathy — Neural Networks: Zero to Hero

data.conclusion: 🎯 Milestone: Build a character-level language model from scratch (following Karpathy). Fine-tune a Hugging Face model on a custom classification task.

data.hypothesis: This phase is your highest-leverage career investment right now. The job market is flooded with people who understand ML theory — it's starved for engineers who can ship RAG systems, agents, and LLM-powered products to production.
data.methodology: Build real projects: a RAG system over actual documents, an agent with tool use, and a fine-tuned model. Deploy each one. Use LangSmith/Langfuse for observability from day one.
findings: Prompt engineering — system prompts, few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured outputs
RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) — vector databases, embeddings, chunking strategies
LLM Agents & tool use — function calling, ReAct, planning patterns
Fine-tuning — LoRA, QLoRA with Unsloth/PEFT (parameter-efficient methods)
Production deployment — FastAPI, Docker, LLM observability (LangSmith/Langfuse)
Evaluation — LLM-as-judge, RAGAS, building eval pipelines
data.conclusion: 🎯 Milestone: Ship a complete RAG application over a real document set. Deploy it with a simple UI. Host on GitHub with a README.

data.hypothesis: A working GitHub project beats a certificate every time. Two strong end-to-end projects will open more doors than 10 course completions. Start applying from month 7 — don't wait until you feel 'ready'.
data.methodology: Polish projects, write about them publicly, and apply broadly. Mock interviews weekly. Target LLM Engineer / ML Engineer roles specifically.
findings: Polish 2–3 portfolio projects with clean READMEs and demos
Write 2–3 blog posts on what you built (Medium, Substack, or LinkedIn)
Update LinkedIn — 'AI/ML Engineer' or 'LLM Engineer' in headline
Mock interviews — LeetCode (medium), ML system design, LLM architecture questions
Target roles: LLM Engineer, ML Engineer, AI Product Engineer, AI Consultant
Job boards: LinkedIn, Wellfound / AngelList
Contribute to 1 open source AI project
Attend local AI/ML meetups

references.text: fast.ai Deep Learning for Coders (free book)

data.conclusion: 🎯 Target: 3 portfolio projects on GitHub, 2 blog posts published, 10+ applications sent, 3+ interviews scheduled.

data.hypothesis: These aren't courses — they're reference hubs you return to constantly. The Illustrated Transformer alone will click differently at Month 1 vs Month 5.
data.methodology: Bookmark all on Day 1. Revisit Jay Alammar's posts after each major concept. Use mlabonne/llm-course as your structured roadmap. Use KalyanKS toolkit when building.
findings: Jay Alammar's blog — best visual explanations of ML concepts (attention, GPT, BERT, embeddings)
Sebastian Raschka — deep technical articles on LLM training, fine-tuning, research papers explained
mlabonne/llm-course — structured roadmap + Colab notebooks: fundamentals → scientist → engineer
KalyanKS toolkit — 120+ LLM libraries organized by category (RAG, agents, eval, infra)
ashishps1/learn-ai-engineering — free structured curriculum; good daily progress tracker
data.conclusion: Return to these references constantly throughout all 9 months. They compound in value as your understanding deepens.
